concepts.title: Geons

position.section_title: A Few Notes About Object Recognition in Humans

concepts.one_liner: Geons are a small set of geometric components, such as blocks and cylinders, used to represent and recognize complex objects.
concepts.content: Biederman postulated that objects are represented by decomposing them into a small set of geometric components, such as blocks, cylinders, and cones, which he called Geons. He derived 36 different Geons that can be discriminated visually. Geons are defined by non-accidental attributes such as symmetry, colinearity, cotermination, parallelism, and curvature. An object is defined by a particular arrangement of a small set of Geons. Object recognition consists of a sequence of stages: (1) edge detection, (2) detection of non-accidental properties, (3) detection of Geons, and (4) matching the detected Geons to stored object representations.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept explains how the human visual system might simplify complex objects into a finite set of manageable parts, making object recognition more efficient and structured.
concepts.recap_md: - Geons are basic geometric primitives like cones and blocks used as building blocks for object representation.

concepts.title: Compositionality in the Visual World

position.section_title: A Few Notes About Object Recognition in Humans

concepts.one_liner: Compositionality in vision involves forming objects from simpler, shared elements like Geons, though it is less rigid than compositionality in language.
concepts.content: One important aspect of Biederman's theory is that objects are formed by compositing simpler elements (Geons), which are shared across many different object classes. Compositionality in the visual world is not as strong as that found in language, where a fixed set of words are composed to form sentences with different meanings. In the visual world, components shared across different object classes will have different visual appearances; for example, the legs of tables and chairs share many properties but are not identical. Geons are effective for representing artificial objects like tables, cabinets, and phones, but they fail when applied to represent "stuff" such as grass, clouds, and water, or highly textured objects like trees or food.
concepts.motivation_md: Compositionality explains how a limited set of components can represent a vast array of objects, though it also highlights the limitations of part-based models when dealing with natural textures.
concepts.recap_md: - Visual compositionality uses shared components across different classes, though their appearance may vary.

concepts.title: Levels of Categorization

position.section_title: A Few Notes About Object Recognition in Humans

concepts.one_liner: Categorization occurs at three levels of abstraction: superordinate, basic-level, and subordinate.
concepts.content:
When working on object recognition, a typical task is to train a classifier to categorize images. A category represents a collection of equivalent objects. Categorization is advantageous because it allows an organism to ignore irrelevant differences between stimuli. Eleanor Rosch proposed that categorization occurs at three different levels of abstraction:

1. **Superordinate level**: Very general categories providing a high degree of abstraction (e.g., Furniture, Tree).
2. **Basic level**: The most common level of abstraction (e.g., Chair, Oak).
3. **Subordinate level**: The most specific level of categorization (e.g., Kitchen chair, White oak).

Two objects belonging to the same superordinate category share fewer attributes than two objects belonging to the same subordinate category.
concepts.motivation_md: Categorization helps organisms process information efficiently by grouping similar objects, reducing the cognitive load of treating every unique stimulus as entirely new.
concepts.recap_md: - The basic level is the most common and intuitive level of abstraction for humans.

The subordinate level of categorization is the most specific one.

concepts.title: Prototypes

position.section_title: A Few Notes About Object Recognition in Humans

concepts.one_liner: Prototypes are the clearest members of a category, used by humans to recognize categories by measuring similarity.
concepts.content: Natural categories tend to be fuzzy at their boundaries and inconsistent in the status of their constituent members. Rosch suggested that categories can be represented by prototypes, which are the clearest members of a category. Humans recognize categories by measuring the similarity of an object to these prototypes. By using prototypes, it is easier to work with continuous categories, as the categories are defined by "clear cases" rather than by their boundaries.
concepts.motivation_md: Because real-world categories often lack sharp boundaries, prototypes provide a central reference point that makes classification more flexible and robust.
concepts.recap_md: - Categories are defined by clear examples (prototypes) rather than rigid boundaries.

concepts.title: Standing vs. Occasion Meaning in Affordances

position.section_title: A Few Notes About Object Recognition in Humans

concepts.one_liner: Objects, like words, have a conventional standing meaning and a context-dependent occasion meaning based on their affordances.
concepts.content:
Object recognition is not always a straightforward categorization task because an object's affordances can change as a function of context. In language, an expression has a standing meaning (its conventional meaning) and an occasion meaning (its particular meaning in a specific context). The same principle applies to visual objects, where the intended use or meaning in a scene may differ from its conventional category.

concepts.title: Image Classification
concepts.one_liner: Image classification is the task of determining if a specific object class is present anywhere within an image.
concepts.content: Image classification is one of the simplest tasks in object recognition. The goal is to determine if object class $c$ is present anywhere in the image ${\bf x}$. While this can be viewed as a machine learning problem focusing on the function $f$, in the context of object understanding, the focus is on the output $\mathbf{y}$. Image classification typically assumes a closed vocabulary of $K$ predefined object classes. The task does not attempt to localize the object or count instances. Mathematically, we build a function that maps the input image ${\bf x}$ into an output vector $\hat {\bf y}$: $$\hat {\bf y} = f({\bf x})$$ The output $\hat {\bf y}$ is a binary response where $1$ indicates the object is present and $0$ indicates it is not.
concepts.motivation_md: Image classification provides a fundamental starting point for computer vision by answering the most basic question of presence or absence before moving to more complex tasks like localization.
concepts.recap_md: - The goal is to identify if a class is present, not where it is or how many there are.

concepts.title: Multiclass Classification
concepts.one_liner: Multiclass classification uses an output vector to indicate the presence or absence of multiple object classes simultaneously.
concepts.content:
(see figure: Image classification: Is there a car in this image?)

In general, we want to classify an image according to multiple classes. This is achieved by having an output vector $\hat {\bf y}$ of length $K$, where $K$ is the number of classes. Each component $c$ of the vector $\hat {\bf y}$ indicates whether class $c$ is present or absent in the image. For example, a training set consists of images and their corresponding class indicator vectors.
concepts.motivation_md: Real-world scenes rarely contain only one type of object; multiclass classification allows a system to recognize a variety of different items within a single framework.

concepts.title: Uncertainty in Classification
concepts.one_liner: Uncertainty modeling in classification outputs the probability of an object's presence rather than a binary yes/no response.
concepts.content: We want to enrich the output so that it represents the uncertainty in the presence of the object. This uncertainty can stem from a model $f_{\theta}$ that is not perfectly accurate, or from a noisy or blurry input image $\mathbf{x}$ where the object is difficult to see. This is formulated as a function $f_{\theta}$ that takes the image ${\bf x}$ and outputs the probability of the presence of each of the $K$ classes. Letting $Y_c \in \{0,1\}$ be a binary random variable indicating the presence of class $c$, we model uncertainty as: $$\begin{aligned} p(Y_c=1 \bigm | \mathbf{x}) &= \hat{y}_c \end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: In real-world applications, it is often more useful to know how confident a system is about a detection than to receive a simple binary answer, especially when dealing with low-quality data.
concepts.recap_md: - Uncertainty can arise from model limitations or poor image quality.

concepts.title: Future Directions in Motion Estimation
concepts.one_liner: Current state-of-the-art motion estimation combines supervised and unsupervised learning, though the search for a perfectly accurate solution continues.
concepts.content: Supervised and unsupervised learning-based methods are now the state-of-the-art in motion estimation. But an accurate solution is still missing. One important question is, do we really need learning in order to solve this problem? Should we abandon the derivation of physically motivated algorithms for motion estimation that require no training? Our answer is that we should pursue both directions of work.
concepts.motivation_md: While deep learning has advanced the field, it is unclear if data-driven methods alone can solve motion estimation or if they should be integrated with classical physical models.

concepts.title: Complexity of Object Recognition
concepts.one_liner: Object recognition complexity varies based on the level of detail required, occlusion, and the influence of social context.
concepts.content: There are many tasks that researchers use to address the problem of recognition. Although the ultimate goal is to tell what something it is by looking at it, the way that you will answer the question will change the approach that you will use. For instance, you could say, "That is a chair" and just point at it, or we could ask you to indicate all of the visible parts of the chair, which might be a lot harder if the chair is partially occluded by other chairs producing a sea of legs. It can be hard to precisely delineate the chair if we cannot tell which legs belong to it. In other cases, identifying what a chair is might be difficult, requiring understanding of its context and social conventions. (see figure: What is a chair? The definition is based on affordances (i.e., something you can sit on) and on social conventions (i.e., some surfaces you can sit on are meant to be used to support other objects...)
concepts.motivation_md: Recognition is not a single task; it ranges from simple categorization to complex part segmentation, and is often complicated by visual clutter and the functional nature of objects.
concepts.recap_md: - Recognition difficulty depends on the specific question asked and the visual context.

concepts.title: Object Localization
concepts.one_liner: Object localization consists of localizing where an object is in an image, typically by finding the image-coordinates of a tight bounding box around each instance.
concepts.content:
For many applications, saying that an object is present in the image is not enough. If a visual system for an autonomous vehicle only tells the navigation system that there is a person in the image, it will be insufficient for deciding what to do. Object localization consists of localizing where the object is in the image. There are many ways one can specify where the object is. The most traditional way of representing the object location is using a **bounding box** (@fig-object_detection_bb), that is, finding the image-coordinates of a tight box around each of the instances of class $c$ in the image $\bf x$.

(see figure: Car localization using bounding boxes. Each instance is shown with a different color.)
concepts.motivation_md: In tasks like autonomous driving, simply knowing an object exists is insufficient; the system must know exactly where the object is located to make navigation decisions.
concepts.recap_md: - Object localization identifies the specific spatial location of an object within an image.

concepts.title: Mathematical Formulation of Object Detection
concepts.one_liner: Object detection is formulated as a function mapping an image to a list of bounding boxes and their associated class vectors.
concepts.content:
We will formulate object detection as a function that maps the input image ${\bf x}$ into a list of bounding boxes $\hat {\bf b}_i$ and the associated classes to each bounding box encoded by a vector $\hat {\bf y}_i$, as illustrated in @fig-object_detection_bb.

(see figure: Car localization using bounding boxes. Each instance is shown with a different color.)

The class vector, $\hat {\bf y}_i$, has the same structure as in the image classification task but now it is applied to describe each bounding box. Bounding boxes are usually represented as a vector of length 4 using the coordinates of the two corners, ${\bf b} = \left[ x_1, y_1, x_2, y_2 \right]$, or with the center coordinates, width, and height, ${\bf b} = \left[ x_c, y_c, w, h \right]$. Our goal is a function $f$ that outputs a set of bounding boxes, $\mathbf{b}$, and their classes $\mathbf{y}$: $$\hat {\bf y}_i, \hat {\bf b}_i = f({\bf x})$$

concepts.title: General Steps for Object Detection
concepts.one_liner: Object detection typically involves proposing candidate boxes, classifying the image patches within them, and postprocessing to remove redundancies.
concepts.content: Most approaches for object detection have three main steps. In the first step, a set of candidate bounding boxes are proposed. In the second step, we loop over all proposed bounding boxes, and for each one, we apply a classifier to the image patch inside the bounding box. In the third and final step, the selected bounding boxes are postprocessed to remove any redundant detections.
concepts.motivation_md: Breaking detection into proposal, classification, and refinement stages makes the complex task of finding objects of any size at any location computationally manageable.

concepts.title: Selective Search
concepts.one_liner: Selective search efficiently proposes candidate bounding boxes using a fast mechanism before applying a more expensive classifier to the selected regions.
concepts.content:
The window scanning approach can be slow as the same classifier needs to be applied to tens of thousands of image patches. Selective search makes the process more efficient by proposing an initial set of bounding boxes that are good candidates to contain an object (@fig-selective_search_pipeline). This proposal mechanism is performed by a selection mechanism simpler than the object classifier. This approach was motivated by the strategy used by the visual system in which attention is first directed toward image regions likely to contain the target. This first attentional mechanism is very fast but might be wrong. Therefore, a second, more accurate but also more expensive, processing stage is required in order to take a reliable decision. The advantage of this **cascade** of decisions is that the most expensive classifier is only applied to a sparse set of locations dramatically reducing the overall computational cost.

The algorithm for selective search only differs from the window scanning approach on how the list of candidate bounding boxes is generated. Some approaches also add a bounding box refinement step. The overall approach is described in algorithm @fig-selective_search.

(see figure: Selective search algorithm.)

This algorithm has four main steps. In the first step, the algorithm uses an efficient window scanning approach to produce a set of candidate bounding boxes. In the second step, we loop over all the candidate bounding boxes, we crop out the box and resize it to a canonical size, and then we apply an object classifier to classify the cropped image as containing the object we are looking for or not. In the third step, we refine the bounding box for the crops that are classified as containing the object. And finally, in the fourth step, we remove low-scoring boxes and we use **nonmaximum suppression** (NMS) to discard overlapping detections likely to correspond to the same object, so as to output only one bounding box for each instance present in the image.

@fig-selective_search_pipeline.

(see figure: A first classifier selects candidate bounding boxes. A second, stronger, classifier makes the final detections (e.g., cars). Nonmaximum suppression (NMS) removes overlapping detections.)

(see figure: Sketch of the selective search architecture. The image is first broken into candidate regions. Then each region is processed individually using a classifier and a regression.)

concepts.title: Nonmaximum Suppression (NMS)
concepts.one_liner: Nonmaximum suppression (NMS) is an iterative algorithm used to discard overlapping bounding boxes by keeping only the highest confidence detections.
concepts.content:
Nonmaximum suppression (NMS) is used to discard overlapping detections likely to correspond to the same object. The nonmaximum suppression algorithm takes as input a set of object bounding boxes and confidences, $S=\{\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \hat{\mathbf{y}}_i\}_{i=1}^B$, and outputs a smaller set removing overlapping bounding boxes. It is an iterative algorithm as follows:
(1) Take the highest confidence bounding box from the set $S$ and add it to the final set $S^*$.
(2) Remove from $S$ the selected bounding box and all the bounding boxes with an IoU larger than a threshold.
(3) Go to step 1 until $S$ is empty.
concepts.motivation_md: Detectors often produce multiple overlapping boxes for the same object; NMS ensures that each physical object is represented by only one bounding box.

concepts.title: Instance Segmentation Loss
concepts.one_liner: The instance segmentation loss is a weighted sum of classification, localization, and segmentation losses.
concepts.content:
The loss can be written as a combination of the classification, localization, and segmentation losses:
$$
\mathcal{L}( \{\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \hat{\mathbf{y}}_i\}, \{\mathbf{b}_i, \mathbf{y}_i\})
     =  \mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i, \mathbf{y}_i) +
     \mathbb{1} (\mathbf{y}_i \neq 0)
     \left( 
     \lambda_1 \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \mathbf{b}_i)
     +
     \lambda_2 \mathcal{L}_{\text{seg}} (\hat{\mathbf{s}}_i, \mathbf{s}_i)
     \right)
$$ 

The first classification loss corresponds to the classification of the crop as containing the object or not. If the object is present, the second term measures the accuracy of the bounding box, and the third term measures whether the segmentation, $\hat{\mathbf{s}}_i$, inside each bounding box matches the ground truth instance segmentation, $\mathbf{s}_i$. The parameters $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ control how much weight each loss has on the final loss.
concepts.motivation_md: To train an instance segmentation model, we need a single scalar loss that penalizes errors in identifying the object class, locating its bounding box, and delineating its specific pixel-level mask simultaneously.
concepts.recap_md:
- The total loss combines classification, localization (bounding box), and segmentation (mask) components.
- A mask loss is only calculated for regions where an object is actually present.
- Hyperparameters $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ balance the relative importance of box accuracy and mask precision.

concepts.title: Limitations of Current Object Representations
concepts.one_liner: Current object representations like bounding boxes and masks are often insufficient for complex tasks like robotics and 3D interaction.
concepts.content:
(see figure: A family of object recognition definitions.)

The representations we have described—image classifiers, region proposals, pixelwise classifiers, and bounding box regression—feel very incomplete. For applications like robotics or autonomous vehicles, these representations are hard to act on. A robot planning to grasp an object needs accurate 3D modeling and an understanding of physical properties to plan grasping points. Similarly, an autonomous vehicle requires a 3D description of object locations and their dynamics. Object segmentation and classification provide only part of the necessary information.

Furthermore, these techniques rely heavily on language to define objects. An advanced computer vision system should behave like a scientist, asking deeper questions about its visual stimuli: Is this piece of matter a distinct object? What is its 3D shape? How is it supported? What are its mechanical properties (e.g., rigid or deformable)? How will it react to external actions? Is it stable, or what will it do next? A system should formulate hypotheses about visual input and perform interventions to answer them, rather than relying solely on language as an internal representation.

concepts.title: Precision-Recall Curve
concepts.one_liner: The precision-recall curve measures the performance of a detection algorithm as a function of the decision threshold.
concepts.content:
The precision-recall curve measures the performance of the detection as a function of the decision threshold. As each bounding box comes with a confidence score $\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i$, we use a threshold, $\beta$, to decide if an object is present at the bounding box location $\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i$ or not. Given a threshold $\beta$, the number of detections is $\sum_i \mathbb{1} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i > \beta)$ and the number of correct detections is $\sum_i \mathbb{1} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i > \beta) \times \mathbf{y}_i$.

From these two quantities we compute the precision as the percentage of correct detections:

$$
Precision(\beta) = \frac{\sum_i  \mathbb{1} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i > \beta) \times \mathbf{y}_i} {\sum_i  \mathbb{1} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i > \beta)}
$$

The precision only gives a partial view on the detector performance as it does not account for the number of ground truth instances that are not detected (misdetections). The recall measures the proportion of ground truth instances that are detected for a given decision threshold $\beta$:

$$Recall (\beta) = \frac{\sum_i  \mathbb{1} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i > \beta) \times \mathbf{y}_i} {\sum_i \mathbf{y}_i}$$

Both precision and recall are quantities between 0 and 1, where high values correspond to high performance. The graph below shows the precision-recall curve as a function of $\beta$.

The precision-recall curve allows practitioners to visualize this trade-off across all possible decision thresholds, helping to select the optimal operating point for a specific application.

concepts.title: Stuff vs. Objects
concepts.one_liner: The distinction between 'objects' with well-defined boundaries and 'stuff' like grass or sky determines whether bounding boxes are an appropriate representation.
concepts.content:
Using bounding boxes to represent the location of objects is not always appropriate, particularly for objects with long, thin structures or regions without well-defined boundaries. It is useful to differentiate between **stuff** and **objects**. Stuff refers to things that do not have well-defined boundaries such as grass, water, and sky. 

However, the distinction is not always sharp. In some images, object instances might be easy to separate, while in others they become a texture where instances cannot be detected individually. In cases with many instances, it may be better to represent the region as a category (e.g., "trees") rather than detecting each instance.

(see figure: Bounding boxes are not an appropriate representation of the location of trees. This is true for many object classes with extended shapes that are hard to approximate with a box.)

Even with few instances, bounding boxes can provide ambiguous localization when objects overlap, making it unclear which pixels belong to which object. Furthermore, bounding boxes are insufficient for tasks like robot manipulation, which require detailed descriptions of pose and shape.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard object detection relies on bounding boxes, but this geometric primitive fails for amorphous regions or complex shapes. Recognizing the difference between 'stuff' and 'objects' helps researchers choose between detection, semantic segmentation, or instance segmentation approaches.

concepts.title: Semantic Segmentation
concepts.one_liner: Semantic segmentation is the process of classifying each pixel in an image with an object class label.
concepts.content:
Semantic segmentation is the per-pixel classification of object labels. Instead of using bounding boxes, which may not well-describe 'stuff' or wiry objects, this approach attempts to classify every pixel in an image.

(see figure: Semantic segmentation. Every pixel is annotated with a semantic tag (red = car, blue = building, green = road, yellow = sidewalk, and cyan = sign).)

In its generic formulation, semantic segmentation takes an image $\mathbf{x}(n,m)$ and outputs a classification vector at each location:
$$\hat{\mathbf{y}} \left[n,m \right] = f(\mathbf{x} \left[n,m \right])$$

This function $f$ is generally implemented as a neural network with an encoder-decoder structure. Alternatively, a window-scanning approach can be used where $f$ outputs the class of the central pixel of an image patch. Training requires a dataset of segmented images with ground truth $y^{(t)}_c \left[n,m \right]$. The multiclass semantic segmentation loss is the cross-entropy loss applied to each pixel:
$$\mathcal{L}_{seg}(\hat{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{y}) = -\sum_{t=1}^{T} \sum_{c=1}^{K} \sum_{n,m}  y^{(t)}_c \left[n,m \right] \log(\hat{y}^{(t)}_c \left[n,m \right])$$

To avoid focusing too much on large objects, classes can be weighted by their average area. Quality is often measured by the average Intersection over Union (IoU) across classes, which is more informative than simple pixel accuracy.

### Shortcomings
This representation cannot count instances; two instances of the same class in contact will appear as a single segment. It also typically labels each pixel with a single class, failing to handle transparencies or depth ordering.
concepts.motivation_md: Bounding boxes are often too coarse for complex shapes or amorphous regions. Semantic segmentation provides a dense, pixel-level understanding of the scene, which is necessary for tasks like autonomous driving where identifying the exact boundaries of the road, sidewalks, and obstacles is vital.

concepts.title: Instance Segmentation
concepts.one_liner: Instance segmentation combines object detection and semantic segmentation to output pixel-level masks for every individual object instance.
concepts.content:
Instance segmentation combines object detection and semantic segmentation to output a set of localized objects represented as pixel-level masks. Unlike semantic segmentation, which provides an aggregate region for a class, instance segmentation can distinguish between $K$ different objects of the same type and delineate overlapping instances.

(see figure: Instance segmentation. Each instance of the class car is assigned to a different color.)

One approach is to use an object localization pipeline to propose bounding boxes, then feed the cropped image within each box to a binary semantic segmentation function. This function predicts whether each pixel in the box $\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i$ belongs to the object.

(see figure: Architecture for instance segmentation. This architecture combines several of the components we have seen previously. The image is first broken into overlapping regions, and then class segmentation...)

The model uses a detector $f_0$ to propose regions and a function $f_1$ to perform classification and segmentation:
$$\left[\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i,   \hat{\mathbf{s}}_i \right]= f_j(\mathbf{x}, \hat{\mathbf{b}}_i)$$
where $\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i$ is the confidence and $\hat{s}_i$ is the mask. The total loss combines classification, localization, and segmentation components:
$$\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}} + \mathbb{1} (\mathbf{y}_i \neq 0) (\lambda_1 \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} + \lambda_2 \mathcal{L}_{\text{seg}})$$

### Shortcomings
While this is a complete representation that can classify, localize, and count, it can be extremely challenging to implement precisely. It also remains limited by its reliance on language to define classes.
concepts.motivation_md: Semantic segmentation fails to distinguish between individual objects of the same class (e.g., a crowd of people), while object detection only provides coarse boxes. Instance segmentation solves both problems by providing precise boundaries for every unique object instance.
concepts.recap_md: - Instance segmentation identifies and masks every individual object separately, even if they belong to the same class.

concepts.title: Cascade of Classifiers
concepts.one_liner: A cascade of classifiers divides object search into a sequence of classifiers with increasing computational complexity and accuracy to efficiently localize objects in images.
concepts.content:
Trying to localize an object in an image is like finding a needle in a haystack: the object is usually small and might be surrounded by a complex background. Selective search reduced the complexity of the search by dividing the search into two steps: a first, fast, and cheap classification function that detects good candidate locations; and a second, slow, and expensive classification function capable of accurately classifying the object that only needs to be applied in a subset of all possible locations and scales. Cascade of classifiers pushes this idea to the limit by dividing the search into a sequence of classifiers of increasing computational complexity and accuracy.

The algorithm for the cascade of classifiers is:

(see figure: Cascade of classifiers algorithm.)

Cascades of classifiers became popular in computer vision when Paul Viola and Michael Jones introduced it in 2001 with a ground-breaking real-time face detector based on a cascade of boosted classifiers. In parallel, Fleuret and Geman also proposed a system that performs a sequence of binary tests at each location. Each binary test checks for the presence of a particular image feature. Early versions of this strategy were also inspired by the game "Twenty Questions".

In a cascade, computational power is allocated into the image regions that are more likely to contain the target object while regions that are flat or contain few features are rejected quickly and almost no computations are allocated in them. The following figure shows a beautiful illustration of how a cascaded classifier allocates computing power in the image when trained to detect faces. The intensity shown in the heat map is proportional to the number of levels in the cascade applied to each location.

(see figure: (left) Input image with the output of a face detector from 1999. (right) The heat map reports the computational cost at each location. Most of the computation was allocated into the wrong detections...)

It is interesting to point out that the scanning window approach ($Levels = 1$) and the selective search procedure ($Levels = 2$) are special cases of this algorithm. The cascade of classifiers usually does not have a bounding box refinement stage as it already started with a full list of all bounding boxes, but it could be added if we wanted to add new transformations not available in the initial set (e.g., rotations).

concepts.title: Object Localization Loss
concepts.one_liner: The object localization loss combines classification and localization tasks into a single objective function to train object detectors end-to-end.
concepts.content:
The object localization loss has to take into account two complementary tasks: classification and localization.

- Classification loss ($\mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}$): For each detected bounding box, does the predicted label match the ground truth at that location?
- Localization loss ($\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}}$): How close is the detected location to the ground truth object location?

For each image, the output of our object detector is a set of bounding boxes $\{\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \hat{\mathbf{y}}_i\}_{i=1}^B$. The first step in the evaluation is to associate each detection with a ground truth label so that we have a set $\{\mathbf{b}_i, \mathbf{y}_i\}_{i=1}^B$. For each of the predicted bounding boxes that overlaps with the ground truth instances, we optimize parameters to improve predicted locations and labels. Predicted bounding boxes that do not overlap with ground truth instances are assigned to the background class, $\mathbf{y}_i=0$, and we optimize the model to reduce their predicted class score, $\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i$.

(see figure: (left) Detector output (using a low threshold to generate many detections). (middle) Ground truth bounding boxes (one color per instance). (right) Detector outputs that overlap with ground truth...)

For the classification loss, we can use the cross-entropy loss:
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i, \mathbf{y}_i) = - \sum_{c=1}^{K} y_{c,i} \log(\hat{y}_{c,i})$$
where $K$ is the number of classes.

For the localization loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \mathbf{b}_i)$, a typical measure is the Intersection over Union (IoU):
[FIGURE:10874378d0fc5d26 | Sketch of the computation of intersection over union for two bounding boxes.]
The loss is defined as $\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}, \mathbf{b})= 1-IoU (\hat{\mathbf{b}}, \mathbf{b})$. Alternatively, the L2 regression loss can be used:
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}, \mathbf{b}) = (\hat{x}_1 - x_1)^2 + (\hat{x}_2 - x_2)^2 + (\hat{y}_1 - y_1)^2 + (\hat{y}_2 - y_2)^2$$

(see figure: (left) Input image with the output of a face detector from 1999. (right) The heat map reports the computational cost at each location. Most of the computation was allocated into the wrong detections...)

The overall loss is computed as:
$$\mathcal{L}( \{\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \hat{\mathbf{y}}_i\}, \{\mathbf{b}_i, \mathbf{y}_i\}) = \mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i, \mathbf{y}_i) + \lambda \mathbb{1} (\mathbf{y}_i \neq 0) \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \mathbf{b}_i)$$
where the indicator function $\mathbb{1} (\mathbf{y}_i \neq 0)$ sets the location loss to zero for bounding boxes that do not overlap with ground truth. The parameter $\lambda$ balances the relative strength of both losses.
concepts.motivation_md: Training an object detector requires optimizing both what an object is and where it is located. A combined loss function allows these two distinct tasks to be optimized simultaneously through backpropagation.

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}, \mathbf{b}) = (\hat{x}_1 - x_1)^2 + (\hat{x}_2 - x_2)^2 + (\hat{y}_1 - y_1)^2 + (\hat{y}_2 - y_2)^2$$

The overall loss is computed as:
$$\mathcal{L}( \{\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \hat{\mathbf{y}}_i\}, \{\mathbf{b}_i, \mathbf{y}_i\}) = \mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i, \mathbf{y}_i) + \lambda \mathbb{1} (\mathbf{y}_i \neq 0) \mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}_i, \mathbf{b}_i)$$
where the indicator function $\mathbb{1} (\mathbf{y}_i \neq 0)$ sets the location loss to zero for bounding boxes that do not overlap with ground truth. The parameter $\lambda$ balances the relative strength of both losses.

concepts.title: Classification Loss
concepts.one_liner: Classification loss measures whether the predicted label for a detected bounding box matches the ground truth label at that location.
concepts.content:
Classification loss ($\mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}$) evaluates if the predicted label matches the ground truth at a specific location for each detected bounding box. Since each bounding box can only have one class, the cross-entropy loss is typically used:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{cls}}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i, \mathbf{y}_i) = - \sum_{c=1}^{K} y_{c,i} \log(\hat{y}_{c,i})$$

where $K$ is the number of classes.
concepts.motivation_md: In object detection, it is not enough to find a box; the system must also correctly identify the category of the object within that box. This loss provides the gradient needed to improve category predictions.

concepts.title: Localization Loss
concepts.one_liner: Localization loss measures how close a detected bounding box is to the ground truth object location.
concepts.content:
Localization loss ($\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}}$) measures the distance between a detected location and the ground truth object location. One typical measure of similarity between two bounding boxes is the Intersection over Union (IoU).

[FIGURE:10874378d0fc5d26 | Sketch of the computation of intersection over union for two bounding boxes.]

The IoU is a quantity between 0 and 1, where 0 means no overlap and 1 means the bounding boxes are identical. The loss can be defined as:
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}, \mathbf{b})= 1-IoU (\hat{\mathbf{b}}, \mathbf{b}).$$

IoU is translation and scale invariant. A simpler alternative is the L2 regression loss:
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}, \mathbf{b}) = (\hat{x}_1 - x_1)^2 + (\hat{x}_2 - x_2)^2 + (\hat{y}_1 - y_1)^2 + (\hat{y}_2 - y_2)^2$$

The L2 regression loss is translation invariant but not scale invariant, meaning the loss is larger for bigger bounding boxes.
concepts.motivation_md: Localization loss is necessary to refine the coordinates of predicted bounding boxes, ensuring they tightly enclose the target objects rather than just roughly overlapping them.
concepts.recap_md: - Localization loss quantifies the spatial error between predicted and ground truth bounding boxes.

concepts.title: L2 Regression Loss
concepts.one_liner: L2 regression loss is a translation-invariant but scale-sensitive metric used to optimize the coordinates of predicted bounding boxes.
concepts.content:
The L2 regression loss is a simple loss function used to optimize bounding box coordinates:
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{loc}} (\hat{\mathbf{b}}, \mathbf{b}) = (\hat{x}_1 - x_1)^2 + (\hat{x}_2 - x_2)^2 + (\hat{y}_1 - y_1)^2 + (\hat{y}_2 - y_2)^2$$

While this loss is translation invariant, it is not scale invariant. Consequently, the L2 loss is larger for big bounding boxes. This can be compared to the IoU loss as a function of relative displacement.
concepts.motivation_md: L2 loss is often easier to optimize than IoU because it has a simple derivative. However, its lack of scale invariance means it may over-prioritize large objects during training.
concepts.recap_md: - L2 loss calculates the sum of squared differences between predicted and ground truth coordinates.

concepts.title: Average Precision-Recall Evaluation
concepts.one_liner: Average Precision (AP) summarizes the precision-recall curve into a single value representing the area under the curve to evaluate object detector performance.
concepts.content:
The most common approach for evaluating object localization is measuring the average precision-recall. This requires assigning detection outputs to ground truth labels, often using the methodology from the PASCAL challenge.

Precision-recall curve measures the performance of the detection as a function of the decision threshold $\beta$. Given a threshold $\beta$, we compute the precision as the percentage of correct detections:

$$Precision(\beta) = \frac{\sum_i  \mathbb{1} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i > \beta) \times \mathbf{y}_i} {\sum_i  \mathbb{1} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i > \beta)}$$

The recall measures the proportion of ground truth instances that are detected for a given decision threshold $\beta$:

$$Recall (\beta) = \frac{\sum_i  \mathbb{1} (\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i > \beta) \times \mathbf{y}_i} {\sum_i \mathbf{y}_i}$$

Both precision and recall are quantities between 0 and 1, where high values correspond to high performance. 

(see figure: Example of a precision-recall curve. This is a standard plot to evaluate detection algorithms. It is usually summarized by the area under the curve. In this example, note that recall stops around...)

The precision-recall curve is non-monotonic. The average precision (AP) summarizes the entire curve with one number, representing the area under the precision-recall curve.
concepts.motivation_md: Detectors produce many candidate boxes with different confidence scores. A single accuracy number isn't enough; we need to understand the trade-off between finding all objects (recall) and ensuring detections are correct (precision) across all possible confidence thresholds.
concepts.recap_md: - Precision is the fraction of detections that are correct, while recall is the fraction of ground truth objects successfully detected.

concepts.title: Assigning Detections to Ground Truth Labels
concepts.one_liner: This procedure matches predicted bounding boxes to ground truth labels by sorting detections by confidence and selecting the highest IoU overlap.
concepts.content:
To assign detections to ground truth labels, follow this procedure for each image:
1. Sort all detections by their confidence score, $\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i$.
2. Loop over the sorted list in decreasing order.
3. For each bounding box, compute the IoU with all ground truth bounding boxes.
4. Select the ground truth bounding box with the highest IoU.
5. If the IoU is larger than a predefined threshold (typically 0.5), mark the detection as correct and remove that ground truth bounding box from the list to avoid double counting.
6. If the IoU is below the threshold, mark the detection as incorrect and do not remove the ground truth label.
7. Repeat until no more detections remain. Mark any remaining ground-truth bounding boxes as missed detections.
concepts.motivation_md: In evaluation, we must decide which predicted box corresponds to which real object. This greedy matching process ensures that each ground truth object is only 'found' once and that high-confidence predictions are prioritized.
concepts.recap_md: - Detections are matched to ground truth based on the highest IoU above a specific threshold.

concepts.title: Exclusive Classes and Simplex Constraint
concepts.one_liner: Multiclass classification with exclusive classes requires that predicted probabilities sum to one, constraining the solution to lie within a simplex.
concepts.content: One common assumption is that only one class, among the $K$ possible classes, is present in the image. This is typical in settings where most of the images contain a single large object. Multiclass classification with exclusive classes results in the following constraint: $$\sum_{c=1}^K \hat{y}_c=1 $$ where $0>\hat{y}_c>1$. In the toy example with three classes shown previously, the valid solutions for $\hat{\mathbf{y}}=[\hat{y}_1, \hat{y}_2, \hat{y}_3]^\mathsf{T}$ are constrained to lie within a simplex. [FIGURE:f4016c609bc00301] Under this formulation, the function $f$ is a mapping $f:\mathbb{R}^{N \times M \times 3} \rightarrow \vartriangle^{K-1}$ from the set of red-green-blue (RGB) images to the $(K-1)$-dimensional simplex, $\vartriangle^{K-1}$.
concepts.motivation_md: This constraint is used when an image is assumed to contain exactly one primary object, ensuring the model's output represents a valid probability distribution over mutually exclusive categories.

concepts.title: Multilabel Classification
concepts.one_liner: When an image can have multiple labels simultaneously, the classification problem can be formulated as a set of binary classification problems.
concepts.content: When the image can have multiple labels simultaneously, the classification problem can be formulated as $K$ binary classification problems (where $K$ is the number of classes). In such a case, the function $f_\theta$ can be a neural network shared across all classes (Figure class_architecture), and the output vector $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$, of length $K$, is computed using a sigmoid nonlinearity for each output class. In this case the output can still be interpreted as the probability $\hat{y}_c = p_\theta(Y_c=1 \bigm | \mathbf{x})$, but without the constraint that the sum across classes is 1. (see figure: Multilabel image classification system.)
concepts.motivation_md: Standard multiclass classification fails when an image contains multiple distinct objects; multilabel classification solves this by allowing each class to be predicted independently.
concepts.recap_md: - Multilabel classification treats each class as an independent binary classification problem.

concepts.title: Misclassification Error
concepts.one_liner: Misclassification error measures the number of incorrect class assignments over a dataset.
concepts.content: A common measure of classification error is the misclassification error. The errors that the function $f$ makes are the number of misplaced ones (i.e., the misclassification error) over the dataset, which we can write as: $$\begin{aligned} \mathcal{L}(\hat{\mathbf{y}},\mathbf{y}) = \sum_{t=1}^T \sum_{c=1}^{K} \mathbb{1}(\hat{y}^{(t)}_c \neq y^{(t)}_c ). \end{aligned}$$ where $T$ is the number of images in the dataset.
concepts.motivation_md: It provides a simple, intuitive metric for evaluating how many individual label assignments a model gets wrong across all samples and classes.
concepts.recap_md: - Misclassification error counts the total number of incorrect predictions in the dataset.

concepts.title: Top-1 Performance
concepts.one_liner: Top-1 performance measures the percentage of times that the true class-label matches the highest scored prediction in the test set.
concepts.content: One way to evaluate a classifier is to rank predicted classes according to their values. The top-1 performance measures the percentage of times that the true class-label matches the highest scored prediction, $\hat{y} = \underset{c}{\mathrm{argmax}} ( \hat{y}_c )$, in the test set: $$\text{TOP-1} = \frac{100}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T \mathbb{1}( \hat{y}^{(t)} = y^{(t)}) $$ where $y^{(t)}$ is the ground truth class of image $t$. This evaluation metric only works for the exclusive class case since we assume a single ground truth class per image. For the multilabel case, we may instead check if each label is predicted correctly.
concepts.motivation_md: It is the most standard and rigorous metric for classification, requiring the model to identify the single correct class as its primary choice.
concepts.recap_md: - Top-1 accuracy checks if the class with the maximum predicted probability is the correct one.

slots.example: One way to evaluate a classifier is to rank predicted classes according to their values. The top-1 performance measures the percentage of times that the true class-label matches the highest scored prediction, $\hat{y} = \underset{c}{\mathrm{argmax}} ( \hat{y}_c )$, in the test set: $$\text{TOP-1} = \frac{100}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T \mathbb{1}( \hat{y}^{(t)} = y^{(t)}) $$ where $y^{(t)}$ is the ground truth class of image $t$. This evaluation metric only works for the exclusive class case since we assume a single ground truth class per image. For the multilabel case, we may instead check if each label is predicted correctly.

concepts.title: Top-5 Performance
concepts.one_liner: Top-5 performance measures the percentage of times that the true label is within the set of five highest scoring predictions.
concepts.content: In some benchmarks (such as ImageNet), researchers also measure the top-5 performance, which is the percentage of times that the true label is within the set of five highest scoring predictions. Top-5 is useful in settings where the labels might be ambiguous, or where multiple labels for one image might be possible. In the case of multiple labels, ideally, the test set should specify which labels are possible and evaluate only using those. The top-5 measure is less precise and it is used when the test set only contains one label despite that multiple labels might be correct.
concepts.motivation_md: It accounts for label ambiguity and near-misses, providing a more lenient evaluation in datasets where images might contain multiple valid objects but only one is labeled.
concepts.recap_md: - Top-5 performance counts a prediction as correct if the true label is in the top five predictions.

concepts.title: Confusion Matrix
concepts.one_liner: The confusion matrix summarizes both the overall performance of the classifier and the percentage of times that two classes are confused.
concepts.content: A confusion matrix is used to understand the structure of mistakes made by a model. The confusion matrix summarizes both the overall performance of the classifier and also the percentage of times that two classes are confused by the classifier. (see figure: Confusion matrix for a three-way classification task. The numbers are percentages.) The diagonal elements are the same as the top-1 performance for each class, while the off-diagonal elements show the confusions. The elements of the confusion matrix are: $$C_{i,j} = 100 \frac{ \sum_{i=1}^N \mathbb{1}( \hat{y}^{(t)} = j) \mathbb{1} (y^{(t)} = i) }{ \sum_{i=1}^N \mathbb{1}(y^{(t)} = i) } $$ where $C_{i,j}$ measures the percentage of times that true class $i$ is classified as class $j$. In this toy example, we can see that 80 percent of the cat images are correctly classified, while 5 percent of cat images are classified as car images, and 15 percent are classified as pictures of dogs.
concepts.motivation_md: It allows researchers to diagnose specific weaknesses in a model by identifying which classes are frequently mistaken for one another.
concepts.recap_md: - The diagonal of the confusion matrix shows the accuracy for each individual class.

concepts.title: Ambiguity in Image Classification
concepts.one_liner: Image classification assumes that we can answer unambiguously whether an image contains a specific object, but class definitions are often ambiguous and boundaries are soft.
concepts.content: The task of image classification assumes that we can answer unambiguously whether an image contains a specific object. However, class definitions are often ambiguous and class boundaries are soft. Even in cases where we believe boundaries are well defined, it is easy to find images that challenge our assumptions. [FIGURE:360abab54729bcf5] [FIGURE:a64dd9969f9fe987] [FIGURE:2e461a626376ea7e] [FIGURE:2f43ff582bf7c58e] [FIGURE:479c0a519751a2ba] [FIGURE:aee6e4196eafb081] Which of these images contains a car? This simple question does not have a simple answer. The top three images contain cars, although with increasing difficulty. For the three images on the second row, it is not clear what the desired answer is. We can recognize the content, but using a single word for describing these images leaves too much ambiguity. Is a car under construction already a car? Is a toy car a car? If we make a car out of watermelon, would that be a car? Language plays a big role in object classification. For example, a pepper is a fruit according to botanics, but a vegetable according to culinary classification. (see figure: A pepper is a fruit according to botanics, and it is a vegetable according to the culinary classification.)
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding these limitations is crucial for developing vision systems that are robust and meaningful in real-world scenarios where categories are not always discrete.
concepts.recap_md: - Classification assumes discrete, unambiguous labels that may not exist in reality.

prereq.rationale: Semantic segmentation is defined as the per-pixel application of classification labels.
This technique is a specific implementation method for the semantic segmentation task.
Instance segmentation is defined as a combination of object detection and semantic segmentation to produce pixel-level masks.
Instance segmentation often uses an object localization pipeline to propose bounding boxes for individual instances.
The loss function is specifically formulated to optimize the multi-task objective of instance segmentation.
The instance segmentation loss incorporates a classification term to determine if a proposed crop contains the target object.
The loss includes a localization term to measure the accuracy of the bounding box for each detected instance.
The critique of current representations assumes an understanding of standard image classification as one of the baseline methods being discussed.
The text explicitly identifies bounding box regression as one of the incomplete representations that is difficult for robots to act upon.
Instance segmentation (pixelwise classification) is cited as a representation that provides only part of the necessary information for complex tasks.
Visual compositionality in Biederman's theory is defined by the arrangement of shared geometric components called Geons.
Prototypes are proposed as the mechanism by which humans represent and recognize the different levels of categories described by Rosch.
The simplex constraint is a specific assumption applied to the multiclass classification problem where only one class is present.
Top-1 performance is a standard metric for evaluating the accuracy of a multiclass classifier.
Object localization extends image classification by adding a spatial component to the task.
The mathematical formulation of detection defines the output as a list of bounding boxes.
These steps provide a high-level procedural framework for implementing object localization.
This approach converts a standard image classifier into a detector by applying it to local windows.
A cascade of classifiers pushes the general idea of a cascade of decisions to its logical limit.
The loss function is used to optimize the parameters of the detection function defined in the formulation.
IoU is a similarity metric specifically designed to compare the overlap between two bounding boxes.
This is the primary methodology used to evaluate the performance of object localization systems.
The assignment procedure relies on IoU to determine if a detection correctly matches a ground truth box.
The curve is generated by varying thresholds on the detections matched to ground truth via the assignment procedure.
Calculating precision requires the set of correct detections determined by the assignment procedure.
Calculating recall requires knowing which ground truth boxes were matched via the assignment procedure.
Average precision is defined as the area under the precision-recall curve.

overlay.rationale: The text contrasts pixel-wise classification with the bounding box approach used in localization.
Semantic segmentation is motivated by the need to describe 'stuff' or wiry objects that bounding boxes handle poorly.
Unlike semantic segmentation, which aggregates regions by class, instance segmentation distinguishes between individual objects of the same type.
Multiclass classification extends the basic binary presence task to handle multiple object categories simultaneously using an output vector.
Multilabel classification explicitly removes the sum-to-one constraint used in exclusive multiclass settings, allowing multiple active labels.
Both are ranking-based evaluation metrics, with Top-5 providing a more lenient measure for ambiguous or multi-label datasets.
The diagonal elements of a confusion matrix represent the Top-1 performance for each individual class.
The inherent ambiguity in class definitions and boundaries motivates the use of probabilistic uncertainty modeling.
Selective search is an efficient alternative to the exhaustive window scanning approach.
Selective search provides a concrete implementation of the cascade of decisions principle.
NMS is the standard algorithm used to perform the third step (postprocessing) of object detection.
L2 regression is a simple, non-scale-invariant alternative for calculating localization loss.
The distinction between stuff and objects helps define the scope where object localization via bounding boxes is appropriate.
